financing.summary: Taylor Morrison was a public builder moving to a land-lighter model until Berkshire Hathaway bought it for $72.50 a share in cash (about $6.8 billion equity, $8.5 billion enterprise value); the merger closed on 2026-07-24 and the company is now a wholly owned Berkshire subsidiary being combined with Clayton Properties Group. Its last public balance sheet (2026-03-31) showed $1.475 billion of senior unsecured notes (2028, 2030, 2032), an undrawn $1.0 billion Wells Fargo-agented revolver to December 2030, $787 million of land-secured project/seller debt and about $1.6 billion of liquidity. Off balance sheet it used land banking heavily: 10,002 for-sale lots ($1.79 billion purchase price) plus 4,476 build-to-rent lots ($980 million) sat in third-party land banks, and for-sale land-bank lots grew from 6,895 (end 2024) even as total controlled lots fell. Kennedy Lewis (manager of Millrose) is the only named land banker, with a $3 billion Yardly build-to-rent facility signed in July 2025 on top of an existing for-sale land-banking agreement. Room for another land banker is now an open question: the controlled share of lots had already slipped from 60% (Sept 2025) to 51% (March 2026) against a stated target of at least 65%, and the new parent holds roughly $350 billion of cash and Treasury bills and could fund land on balance sheet. Taylor Morrison stopped SEC reporting in August 2026, so no lot or debt data newer than 2026-03-31 is public.
financing.land_strategy: Mixed, moving land-lighter until the buyout. The FY2025 10-K describes an asset-light approach that finances land through land banking arrangements, joint ventures, seller financing and option contracts, with the goal of raising the share of homebuilding lots controlled rather than owned. At its March 2025 Investor Day the company set a target of at least 65% of homebuilding lots controlled (alongside about 20,000 closings by 2028). Actual controlled share peaked at 60% (June and Sept 2025), then fell to 54% at year-end 2025 and 51% at 2026-03-31 as total lots dropped from about 85,000 to 75,626. Strategy under Berkshire ownership has not been publicly stated. Within the controlled bucket the mix shifted toward land banking: land-bank lots rose from 6,895 (2024-12-31) to 8,498 (2025-12-31) and 10,002 (2026-03-31), while option-contract lots and other controlled lots (single takedowns, JV share) fell from 42,540 to 28,942.

lots.source_title: Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 (filed 2026-04-22)
lots.note: Latest public quarter (company deregistered in August 2026 after the Berkshire buyout). total_controlled = owned + controlled homebuilding lots. Owned 36,682 = 15,732 undeveloped, 8,000 under development, 12,950 finished. Controlled 38,944 = 6,193 under land option purchase contracts, 10,002 under land banking arrangements, 22,749 other (single-transaction takedowns and the company's share of unconsolidated JV lots). Q1 2026 earnings release states 51% controlled and 6.2 years of supply on trailing-twelve-month closings, of which 3.0 years owned. Trend from earnings releases: 85,051 lots / 60% controlled (2025-06-30); 84,564 / 60% (2025-09-30); 78,835 / 54% (2025-12-31); 75,626 / 51% (2026-03-31). Build-to-rent (Yardly) land-bank lots (4,476) are reported separately and are not in these totals. Aggregate purchase price of assets under option contracts and land banking: $3.4 billion; land deposits on balance sheet: $388.3 million. Year-end comparison (FY2025 10-K inventory note): owned 36,009 and controlled 42,826 at 2025-12-31 (options 8,632; land banking 8,498; other 25,696) versus owned 36,718 and controlled 49,435 at 2024-12-31 (options 9,529; land banking 6,895; other 33,011).

land_banking.description: $3 billion land and construction financing facility dedicated to Yardly, Taylor Morrison's build-to-rent business. It funds existing and new land acquisition, land development and home construction, moves Yardly assets off Taylor Morrison's balance sheet and supports later asset sales. Kennedy Lewis's Darren Richman (also CEO of Millrose Properties) described it as another use case for land banking.

ma.description: All-cash acquisition at $72.50 per share (about $6.8 billion equity value, $8.5 billion enterprise value, 24% premium). Agreement signed 2026-05-31; HSR waiting period expired 2026-07-06; stockholders adopted the agreement on 2026-07-22 (75.8 million votes for, 2.3 million against); closed 2026-07-24. Taylor Morrison is now a wholly owned Berkshire subsidiary and will be combined with Clayton Properties Group.
ma.map_impact: Ownership changes from public (TMHC) to subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway; no more SEC filings, so lot, debt and officer disclosures stop at mid-2026. Taylor Morrison (Builder 100 #6) and Clayton Properties Group (#12) become one Berkshire site-built platform: nearly 23,000 closings in 2025, 21 states, 52 markets, 700+ communities, described as the fourth-largest US homebuilding operation. Sheryl Palmer stays CEO and leads the integration from Scottsdale; brands (Taylor Morrison, Esplanade, Yardly) are kept. The post-closing Taylor Morrison board is Sheryl Palmer, Todd Merrill, Curt VanHyfte and Erik Heuser; the independent directors resigned. Land and finance decision rights may shift toward Berkshire/Clayton, and the need for third-party land banking may fall.
ma.source_title: Berkshire Hathaway Completes Acquisition of Taylor Morrison (8-K Ex. 99.1)
ma.note: Board changes and dates from the 8-K filed 2026-07-24; premium from the 2026-05-31 announcement. Greg Abel negotiated for Berkshire. The proxy says several other parties were sounded out between January and May 2026 and none made a proposal.

ma.counterparty: Undisclosed bidder ("Party A" in the merger proxy)
ma.description: Unsolicited proposal to buy Taylor Morrison for $71.00 per share, 90% in cash and 10% in the bidder's stock. The board rejected it on 2025-12-09, citing valuation and the leverage of the combined company, and talks ended on 2025-12-16.
ma.map_impact: None directly. Shows Taylor Morrison was in play before Berkshire, and that a stock-paying strategic buyer was interested; the bidder's identity is not public.
ma.note: Party A's CEO had met Sheryl Palmer at an industry conference on 2025-09-11.
